summary: For ages 9–11, this guidance teaches the CAUSES of rainforest deforestation as an economic chain (demand → land cleared for a cash product → forest lost), with cattle ranching named as the Amazon's single largest driver, alongside soy, palm oil, logging and mining. It teaches the SCALE (gross deforestation ~10–11 million hectares worldwide per year, made concrete by comparison to a familiar country's area, with the note that the rate is currently falling) and links three impacts via their mechanisms: habitat loss → biodiversity, carbon release → climate, land taken → indigenous peoples. A manipulable land-use model is the lead activity; a reveal infographic, a sort-and-estimate practice task, an optional 3D flythrough, and (deferred) stakeholder dialogue are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.
misconceptions: 'Deforestation is mostly people chopping wood for firewood' — the big drivers are commercial cattle, soy, palm oil, logging and mining.
'The whole rainforest will be gone next year' — the scale is huge but it is a percentage per year, and the rate is currently falling.
'Tree-cover loss and deforestation are the same' — some loss (fire, selective logging) regrows; deforestation is permanent land-use change.
'It only harms animals' — it also releases carbon (climate) and displaces indigenous communities.
'Trees just grow back quickly' — cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its biodiversity.

activities.title: Land-use control panel: build the forest loss from ordinary demands
steps: Play the role of a developer on a map of a rainforest region: allocate patches of land to cattle pasture to meet beef demand, then add soy and palm plots, then logging and mining.
Watch linked meters recompute live as you clear land — forest area falls, a biodiversity/species meter drops, a CO2-released gauge climbs, and a marker shows a displaced community.

Play a year-timeline forward and watch the forest visibly shrink while a running total ticks upward; note that the worldwide annual total is about 10 million hectares a year, so the regional model shows how such demands accumulate.
Compare that worldwide annual total to a familiar country's area (e.g. roughly the size of Portugal or Iceland).

Switch on a second set of controls — regrowth and protected areas — and watch protected areas reduce how much forest is cleared each year (gross loss), while regrowth makes NET loss smaller than gross loss; note that the real worldwide deforestation rate has slowed over recent decades but is still high.
activities.insight: Deforestation is not random destruction but the sum of ordinary DEMANDS — beef, soy, palm, timber, minerals — each trading a patch of irreplaceable forest for a product; the totals are staggering yet changeable, and gross loss differs from net loss once regrowth is counted.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal driver infographic with before/after and scale comparison
steps: Tap each driver hotspot (cattle, soy, palm oil, logging, mining) to reveal its share and the mechanism by which it clears forest.
Swipe a before/after satellite pair of a cleared region to see the change directly.
Study a scale visual showing '≈10.9 Mha worldwide per year = an area this big' set against a map of a familiar country.
activities.insight: In the Amazon and many tropical regions the major drivers are commercial land uses producing for national and export markets (not mainly firewood), and the annual worldwide scale is enormous but comparable to a real country's footprint.

activities.title: Sort the causes and estimate the annual scale
steps: Sort a set of cards into the main commercial drivers of Amazon and tropical deforestation (cattle, soy, palm, logging, mining) versus minor causes like 'villagers gathering firewood'.
Use a slider to estimate how many hectares of forest are lost worldwide each year, then compare your estimate against the real figure (~10–11 million ha/year gross worldwide).
Answer short questions matching each impact to its mechanism: habitat loss → biodiversity, carbon release → climate, land taken → indigenous peoples.
Decide whether two scenarios are both 'deforestation': a patch logged that regrows over 30 years versus a patch turned permanently into a cattle ranch — and explain why.
State the driver→product→forest-loss chain in your own words for one driver.
activities.insight: Learners can identify the dominant commercial drivers, place the annual worldwide scale, and distinguish permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss that regrows.

activities.title: Optional: 3D flythrough over cleared vs intact forest
steps: View or navigate a 3D flythrough that passes over cleared land beside intact rainforest to see the contrast directly.
Relate what you see to the drivers and quantities studied in the other activities — which demands drove this clearance, and how it adds to the annual total.
activities.insight: Seeing cleared versus intact forest in 3D can make the loss vivid, while the core learning remains the drivers and quantities behind it.

activities.title: Optional: competing stakeholders (deferred extension)
steps: Hear from or role-play a rancher, a logger and a conservationist, each stating their motives for and against clearing forest.
Identify the competing demands and trade-offs behind a single cleared patch.
activities.insight: Behind forest loss sit real people with competing economic motives; deforestation decisions involve trade-offs, not simple villains.

checkQuestion: A lot of people think rainforests are mostly cut down by poor villagers gathering firewood. Is that the main cause of large-scale deforestation? Tell me yes or no, then tell me what the biggest causes really are and WHY.
checkAnswer: No — firewood-gathering is not the main cause. Most large-scale deforestation is commercial: clearing land for cattle ranching (the biggest driver in the Amazon), soy and palm oil plantations, logging for timber, and mining — clearing huge areas for profit and export. Roughly 10 million hectares of forest are lost worldwide each year, harming biodiversity, the climate, and indigenous communities.
